n: Joshua calls together the two and a half tribes whose land lay east of the Jordan. They had crossed over to help their brothers conquer Canaan.
Joshua praises them for keeping their promise to Moses and following his own orders faithfully.
For years they had fought beside the other tribes instead of going home. Their loyalty kept Israel united.

f.g: Carried out the duty entrusted to them.

n: With the land at rest, Joshua releases them to go home to their families across the Jordan.

f.g: Go home (an idiom from Israel’s tent-dwelling days).

n: Joshua’s parting charge sums up the whole law: love God, walk in His ways, keep His commandments, cling to Him, and serve Him with all your heart. Distance from the tabernacle must not mean distance from God.

f.w: to love the LORD your God

f.g: Hold fast to Him, as in a close bond.

n: Joshua gives them a blessing as they leave, as a father would to departing sons.

f.g: A formal spoken blessing invoking God’s favor.

n: The text explains that Manasseh was split: half had land in Bashan from Moses, half west of the Jordan from Joshua. Joshua blesses the eastern half too.
They return rich with spoil and are told to share it with those who stayed home — a principle of fairness already set by Moses and later by David.

f.g: Clothing.

n: The eastern tribes leave Shiloh and head toward Gilead, their land east of the Jordan.

f.g: The highlands east of the Jordan River.

n: At the Jordan they build a huge altar, built to be seen from far away. Its purpose isn’t yet explained, which sets up the crisis that follows.

f.w: a great altar to see to
f.g: An altar impressive to look at — conspicuous.

n: News spreads to the other tribes that an altar has been built at the river crossing, on the border of Canaan.

f.g: Facing, opposite.

n: The western tribes gather to go to war. The law allowed only one altar for sacrifice, so a second altar looked like rebellion against God.

f.w: to go up to war against them

n: Wisely, they first send a delegation led by Phinehas, the zealous priest who had once stopped a plague by standing for the Lord.
Ten leaders, one from each western tribe, go with Phinehas, so the whole nation speaks together.

f.g: The clans or military divisions of Israel.

n: The delegation reaches Gilead and confronts the eastern tribes face to face. Talking first prevents a needless war.
The delegates accuse them of turning from the Lord by building a rival altar.

f.g: Hebrew ma‘al, a breach of faith, betraying a trust.

n: They recall the sin at Peor, where Israel worshiped Baal and a plague followed. They fear history repeating.
Israel saw itself as one covenant people; one group’s rebellion could bring God’s judgment on all.

f.g: Angry.

n: They make a generous offer: if your land feels spiritually unclean, come live with us near the tabernacle — just don’t build a rival altar.

f.g: Ritually impure; lacking the Lord’s sanctuary.
The land west of the Jordan, where the tabernacle stood.

n: They recall Achan, whose secret sin brought defeat on all Israel. One person’s choices can affect the whole community.

f.g: Things devoted to God that were forbidden to be taken.

n: The eastern tribes answer the leaders.

f.g: Clan leaders.

n: They make a solemn oath, calling on God twice by three titles: God knows our hearts. If we rebelled, don’t spare us.

f.g: Hebrew El, Elohim, Yahweh — three names for God, repeated for emphasis.

n: They insist the altar was never meant for sacrifices; if it were, let the Lord Himself punish them.

f.g: A grain offering; “meat” in KJV often means food in general.
Hold us accountable.

n: Their real fear: someday the western tribes’ children might say the eastern tribes have no part in the Lord.

f.w: What have ye to do with the LORD God of Israel?
f.g: That is, “You aren’t really part of God’s people.”

n: The Jordan River could become a spiritual dividing line. They worried their children might be shut out and stop fearing the Lord.

f.g: Stop worshiping and revering the Lord.

n: So they built an altar not to use, but as a monument.
The altar stands as a witness that they also belong to the Lord and will worship at His true sanctuary.

f.g: Hebrew ‘ed, a testimony or evidence.

n: It is a replica, a “pattern” of the Lord’s altar, so future generations can point to it as proof of their shared faith.

f.g: A model or copy.

n: They firmly reject any thought of building a competing place of sacrifice. They honor the one altar before the tabernacle.

f.g: An emphatic “Far be it from us!”

n: Phinehas and the leaders are satisfied. A careful hearing turned suspicion into understanding.

f.g: Literally, “it was good in their eyes.”

n: Phinehas rejoices that the Lord is still with Israel; the eastern tribes have kept the whole nation safe from judgment.
The delegation returns and reports back to the tribes at Shiloh.

f.g: Reported back.

n: Israel praises God and drops plans for war. Conflict was avoided because people listened before acting.

f.g: Praised God.

n: The eastern tribes name the altar “Witness”: a reminder that the Lord is God for both sides of the Jordan.

f.g: Hebrew “witness.” The word is missing in many Hebrew manuscripts and supplied by translators.
